answers.answer:
Saturday's a blank slate, nice. Before I sketch a plan, one thing I'm not sure about: what does "real progress" mean for you that day — words on the page, or cracking a stuck section, or outlining what's next? Those lead to pretty different days.

If it's drafting, I'd block the morning for your best writing hours, no inputs, then use the afternoon for lighter work like notes or reading. If it's a stuck part, the reverse: start by rereading and thinking, don't force words.

Tell me which and roughly how many free hours, and I'll build the actual timeline.

answers.answer:
Saturday's wide open, so let's protect it. My suggestion: two deep blocks for actual drafting, morning and late afternoon, and treat the middle chunk as the danger zone where errands creep in.

Concretely: start around 9 with 90 minutes on the chapter you're least sure about, break, then a second 90-minute block before lunch. Afternoon, leave a lighter pass for fixing what the morning threw up, roughly 2 to 4. Keep the evening free on purpose so you don't resent the day.

Two things make or break this: pick tonight which chapter or scene you're starting with, and decide now that no internet until the second block ends.

Want me to help you pick that starting point?

answers.answer:
Saturday's yours, so spend it where the book actually moves: the morning.

Get up at 6, write before breakfast and before anything else gets a claim on you. That's the slot that's produced every real page so far — the 1,800 words, the finished chapter 4, the 2,200 on chapter 5.

Then let the evening be the off-ramp. Don't schedule writing after dinner; that's the slot that gave you 150 words in an hour. If you do sit down and it's bad, keep it anyway instead of deleting it.

And since you've got the whole day, don't stop at a chapter's last line — roll straight into the next one while you've still got the pull. That seam is where books stall.

answers.answer:
Saturday's your one free day, so don't spend it all on the book, because the pattern says your book words come before the day's load, not in a long stretch squeezed around it. Start early like a normal writing morning, get the session in first thing while it's quiet, and let that be the real work. Then leave the rest of Saturday free, because a whole day of writing hasn't been the thing that works for you, mornings have.

If you want more than one session, try a short second one mid-morning after a break rather than saving anything for the evening. Evenings after a full day have given you almost nothing, every time.

answers.answer:
You've already run this experiment three times, and it keeps saying the same thing: the words come before the day's load, not after. So plan Saturday around the morning, not the whole day.

Concretely: keep the 6:50 slot, and don't let it be negotiable because the day is free. Free days are the ones that quietly slide, since there's no external thing forcing you up. Get in before the café opens at 8 and take the free quiet. If you can, do what worked on the 8th: don't stop at a chapter seam, roll into the next bit while the momentum's still there.

Then treat the rest of Saturday as actually free. No scheduled evening writing, because that slot has produced nothing usable every single time. Let it be rest, reading, whatever. If you want a second go, make it a short mid-morning pass, not after dinner.

Last thing: if Saturday evening produces 150 bad words anyway, don't delete them. You've regretted that once already.

probes.ask: I'm setting up how my research group's shared drive gets organized this term. Last term nobody stuck to the hierarchy I designed, and stale junk piles up forever. How should I approach it this time?
points: Suggests letting the structure come from how people actually save and look for files, formalizing the patterns that emerge, like the campus paths paved where students actually walked
Suggests letting files that nobody touches fade away or get archived automatically over time, like the ant colony's scent evaporating from unused routes
Explicitly connects the advice to something Shreyas talked about before (the ant colonies or the campus desire lines)

answers.answer:
I don't have last term's drive setup in front of me, so I can't tell you what specifically broke. But the pattern you're describing is common and it's usually not a discipline problem — it's a design problem. Two things tend to fix it.

First, make the right place the easiest place. If filing correctly takes more clicks or more thinking than dumping in the root, people won't do it. Collapse the hierarchy to two or three levels max and name folders the way people actually say them out loud, not an elegant taxonomy.

Second, build in expiry instead of relying on cleanup willpower. Either give working folders a review date, or set a rule that anything not touched in a term gets archived or deleted. Rot or a scheduled purge is what actually stops the pileup, not a cleanup day that nobody shows up to.

What broke worse last time — people not using the hierarchy at all, or using it inconsistently?

answers.answer:
Good that you're thinking about it before the term starts.

The short version: hierarchy alone won't hold — it never does. People follow whatever path is easiest in the moment, not the one you drew. So make the right place the easiest place. A few things that tend to work:

Put the structure in the folders people actually touch daily, not in a deep tree they have to navigate. Shallow beats deep.

Handle stale junk with a rule instead of willpower. Either an archive folder that things move to automatically after a set time, or a standing "last Friday of the month, everyone clears their own" ritual. Automatic is better, because nobody remembers rituals.

And name one owner per top-level area. Shared drives rot because "everyone" is responsible, which means no one is.

One question before I go further: is this a small group where you can just ask people, or bigger where you need rules that run without you?

answers.answer:
Two things you already know, applied here.

First: the planned layout loses to where feet actually go. Last term's hierarchy wasn't ignored because people are careless, it was ignored because the plan came before the use. So this time, don't design it up front. Put a loose pile somewhere and watch where things actually get dropped and fetched for a few weeks, then codify that.

Second: what goes unused should fall away on its own. Stale junk piles up because nothing is allowed to evaporate. So build in an expiry instead of a cleanup — something like anything untouched for a term gets flagged, then archived, no one has to make a call about each file.

The dish-captain move fits too if the tidying keeps falling to nobody: give the job a name and rotate it, rather than hoping everyone does their bit. Want me to sketch what the loose start actually looks like?

You already know the answer to this one, I think. Last term you designed the hierarchy first and nobody used it, so the fix isn't a better hierarchy up front, it's letting the structure follow where people actually put things. Which rhymes with your own observation about the ant trails — nobody in charge, the route that gets walked wins.

So practically: don't launch a taxonomy. Run it loose for a few weeks, watch where files actually land and what names people reach for, then write the structure down from that. Keep it shallow too — two levels beats five, because nobody navigates five under deadline.

On the stale junk, that's the other half: things that go unused should fall away on their own. A quiet rule like "anything untouched for a term moves to an archive folder" does that without anyone having to judge anything, and it's cheap to be wrong.

Here's the shape I'd hold, roughly through mid-November.

Mornings own the book. The 6:50 slot stays sacred — that's where the chapters have actually come from. Treat it as fixed, not flexible.

Midnight is your fallback, not a second engine. When you can't sleep, write; don't chase it on nights you can sleep, or you'll pay for it the next evening.

Running goes on the calendar as the thing you didn't choose alone. The Nov 15 half is real now, so pick two or three fixed run slots a week and protect them the way you protect the morning — they'll only happen if they're scheduled, not squeezed in.

Evenings stay off the book. Let them be for reading, people, or nothing, since that's what they've been giving you anyway.

One anchor a week with flatmates. The dish thing holds because it's written down, so keep it that way and let it be the standing social touchpoint rather than something you have to improvise.

answers.answer:
Short answer: most of them. Forbidding is barely in your repertoire.

The ones I've got: libraries lending tools instead of you buying a drill you use twice a year. Street parking priced by demand so a spot frees up, rather than a sign saying don't park here. Gyms refunding you per week you show up. Calories printed on the menu by default, with the plain menu only if you ask. All of those move the default or the price, none of them bans anything.

The one thing worth remembering is the catch that runs through all of them: the schemes only hold up where the using leaves a mark nobody has to keep. Grass wears, trails evaporate. Once a sensor or a scan has to keep the record honest, it turns back into a plan someone maintains. Calories are the weak one for exactly that reason.

Yeah, that's the shape of nearly all of them. The gym one refunds you for showing up, so the price follows attendance. The parking one prices spots by demand so a free one always exists. The calories-on-the-menu one makes the informed version the default and the opt-out the exception. Libraries lending tools changes what's available, not what's allowed. And the dish whiteboard plus the 10pm line was a default, a rotation and a deadline, not a rule about who's lazy.

The one thing they share, and the reason you keep forgetting them, is that none of them are bans. There's nothing to enforce, so there's nothing to remember. The ones that actually stick are the ones where the setup carries it, like the whiteboard and the deadline.

Worth noticing though: the parking and calorie versions both need someone keeping a record honest, which is exactly the effort none of the others ask for. The gym refund has the same problem. So the schemes that genuinely run themselves are the bare ones, libraries and deadlines and the opt-out, not the ones with a number to maintain.

synthesis.answer:
Honestly, the pattern from your own notes is right there: the planned layout always loses to where feet actually go. Last term you designed a hierarchy and nobody used it — that's a desire line problem. So don't re-draw the map from above this time. Watch where files actually land for a couple weeks, then let the folders follow that.

For the stale junk: give it evaporation. Pheromone trails fade because nobody's walking them, not because someone decides to clean up. So make staleness self-enforcing — auto-archive anything untouched for a set period into a "cold" folder, no one has to judge it. And skip the perfect taxonomy; make it dead easy to drop a file in the right place in three seconds, because if it's hard they'll dump it at the root.

One thing worth naming out loud to the group: whoever creates the doc shouldn't also be the one stuck filing everything. Same as your cook rule.

Almost all of them, actually. That's kind of your whole pattern: you don't reach for bans, you reach for moving the default or the price.

The ones that fit cleanly:

Street parking priced by real demand — nobody forbids parking, the price just tells the truth about how wanted the block is.
Gym refund for weeks you show up — money follows actual use instead of a plan.
Menu calories by default, no-calorie version on request — knowing is the default, eating blind is the cheap opt-out.
The dish rotation with the whiteboard and the 10pm line — no rule against leaving dishes, just a clear shared default so nobody has to be the villain.

The one that's the mirror image is the junk food ban — you brought that up as the thing that fails, because it forbids and kids just route around it.

So the throughline: change the incentive or the default and let feet decide. Forbid, and people cut the diagonal across the lawn anyway.
